text: Marisol Ortega was still in her gardening gloves when Mr. Pruitt leaned over the hedge and asked, almost shyly, whether she'd mind a fence going in along the property line. She laughed so suddenly that a sparrow burst out of the lilac. "Mind? Hector, I've been praying for one since your terrier dug up my dahlias." He grinned and admitted the terrier was the whole reason. They stood there trading ideas like kids planning a fort: cedar or pine, a little gate between the yards so she could still pass him zucchini in August, maybe a trellis on her side for the climbing roses she had always wanted. Marisol kept nodding, her cheeks warm, already picturing pink blooms spilling over the slats by next June. When he went back inside she stayed out longer than she needed to, humming, pacing out the line with her heel and marking spots for the roses with sticks. That night she pulled up a nursery catalog and dog-eared six pages before bed, still smiling at the ceiling in the dark.

I'd been dreading the knock, honestly, because the last neighbor who came to my door with a clipboard wanted to complain about my wind chimes. But Devraj stood on the porch with a box of jalebi and a hand-drawn sketch of a fence, and he asked if we could split the cost and build it together over a weekend. Together. I hadn't built anything with another person since my father passed. I heard myself say yes before he finished the sentence, and my voice came out higher than usual, almost a squeak. We sat on my steps eating the sweets, sticky syrup on our fingers, arguing pleasantly over post spacing. He wanted eight feet; I insisted on six so it would look tidier, and he threw up his hands and laughed and said fine, six. Saturday morning I was up before my alarm, coffee brewed, work gloves laid out on the counter like a kid's first-day-of-school clothes. By noon our shirts were soaked and the first three posts stood straight as soldiers, and I couldn't stop grinning at them.

Old Walter Kim had lived beside the empty lot for eleven years, so when the young couple who finally bought it walked over to ask about putting up a fence, he insisted they come inside first for barley tea. He set out his good cups, the ones with the cranes, and listened as they explained: a low picket fence, nothing to block the sun from his persimmon tree. Walter's eyes crinkled. He told them about the persimmons, how the tree overproduced every autumn and he never knew what to do with the extra fruit. The wife, Priyanka, said she made a wonderful persimmon bread. Walter actually clapped once, a sharp, bright pop that made the husband jump and then laugh. They walked the property line together afterward, Walter pointing with his cane, chattering more than he had in months. When they left, he stood at his window watching them measure the ground, rocking slightly on his heels, and decided that this year he would not let a single persimmon go to waste.

The surveyor's flags were bright orange, and I kept looking out the kitchen window at them like they were party decorations. Agnieszka from next door had asked me last week, very formally, if I would object to a fence, and I had nearly hugged her. My twins are four, and they bolt. Every afternoon in the yard has been me sprinting after one of them toward the street while the other eats dirt. A fence meant I could sit down. I could drink a whole cup of tea while it was still hot. When the crew arrived this morning I made them sandwiches, which they clearly didn't expect, and I hovered on the patio watching the auger bite into the soil. Each post that went in felt like a weight sliding off my shoulders. The twins pressed their faces to the window, narrating every move of the machinery, and I narrated along with them, louder than they were. When the last panel clicked into place I walked the entire perimeter, running my hand along the boards, laughing to myself like a fool.

Tomás had expected a fight. Everyone on Linden Street said Mrs. Abernathy fought about everything, from parking to leaves. So he rehearsed his fence speech for two days, printed the plans, even brought a copy of the plat map. She opened the door, glanced at the papers, and said, "Oh, thank heavens, I was going to ask you." Tomás blinked at her. Then he started to laugh, a real belly laugh that bent him forward, and after a second she joined in, wheezing, holding the doorframe. It turned out she'd been wanting privacy for her bird feeders, which his cat had been terrorizing. They spent half an hour at her kitchen table choosing a stain color, and she showed him photos of a cardinal pair she'd been watching all spring. Walking home, Tomás felt light enough to bounce. He texted his wife three exclamation points and nothing else, then turned around on the sidewalk to wave back at Mrs. Abernathy, who was still standing on her porch, waving too.

My neighbor Femi is a carpenter, and when he told me he wanted to build a fence between our yards, I assumed it would be the ordinary kind. Then he showed me the drawing. Every third board had a small round window cut into it at different heights, one low enough for a child, one at my eye level, one up high where the morning light would pour through. "So we can still see each other," he said, shrugging like it was nothing. I couldn't speak for a second. My throat went tight and warm, and then a laugh came bubbling up out of me. I told him it was the most beautiful fence I had ever heard of. He spent three weekends on it, and I brought out lemonade every afternoon and sat in my lawn chair watching, offering useless advice that he pretended to consider. Now in the evenings I'll be watering my beans and catch his face in one of the little windows, and we both start grinning before either of us says a word.

The envelope had the property management logo on it, and Keisha's stomach tightened out of habit as she slid her thumb under the flap. Rent increases always came in envelopes like this. But the letter said the building had been sold to a tenant cooperative, and that she, as a resident of more than five years, was being offered a share at a price she read three times to be sure. She sat down hard on the stairs. Then she stood up again because sitting felt impossible, and walked a slow circle around her tiny living room, touching things: the radiator that clanked, the window that stuck, the shelf she had hung crooked. All of it could be partly hers. She called her mother and could barely get the words out between laughs, and her mother started laughing too without even knowing why. Keisha spent the evening knocking on neighbors' doors with the letter in her hand, and by nine o'clock there were six of them crowded in the hallway, passing around a bottle of cheap sparkling wine.

I opened the landlord's letter standing at the mailbox, expecting the usual notice about the boiler inspection. Instead, Mr. Castellano had written by hand, in his slanted old-fashioned script, that he was retiring to Sicily and wanted to thank me for being the best tenant he had ever had. He was keeping my rent the same for the next three years, written right into a new lease, and he had arranged for the new manager to honor it. At the bottom he'd added, "Please keep the basil alive on the fire escape. It was my wife's." I read it right there on the sidewalk while a delivery guy tried to get around me. My face hurt from smiling. Upstairs, I went straight to the fire escape and watered the basil even though I had watered it that morning, then pinched off a leaf and smelled it, grinning like an idiot. I wrote him back that same night, three pages, and promised to send photos of the basil every summer until one of us couldn't anymore.

Bartholomew Nwosu was a graduate student who had lived for two years with a refrigerator that hummed like a dying engine and an oven that only worked on the left side. He'd sent four requests. So when the landlord's letter arrived announcing a full kitchen renovation, new appliances, at no cost to tenants, with a hotel stipend for the two days of work, he did a little shuffle step right there in the narrow hallway. His roommate came out to see what the noise was and found him holding the letter over his head like a trophy. "An oven," Bartholomew said. "A whole oven, Lukas. Both sides." They spent the rest of the evening making a list of everything they would cook, which quickly became absurd: roast duck, a croquembouche, bread from scratch. Bartholomew kept getting up from the couch to open the old fridge and say goodbye to it in a dramatic voice. He fell asleep that night with the letter on his nightstand, and when he woke up he reached over and read it again.

When I saw the letter from the landlord about my lease, my first thought was that I'd done something wrong. I'm seventy-three and I play the piano in the evenings, and I worried a neighbor had complained. But the letter was from Ms. Haddad, who owns the building, and it said that several tenants had asked whether I might give lessons to their children in the community room on Saturdays, and would I like to have my rent reduced in exchange. Several tenants. Asked. I had to set the paper down on the piano because my hands had started to tremble, not from worry, from something bright and fizzing in my chest. I've taught no one in fifteen years. I sat down and played the first thing my fingers found, a silly ragtime piece, and played it far too fast and missed half the notes and did not care at all. Then I dug out my old lesson books from the closet, blew the dust off, and stayed up past midnight planning which songs a seven-year-old would love.

Rosalind had been bracing for the lease renewal letter all month. Her dog, a lumbering mastiff mix named Biscuit, was technically over the building's weight limit, and she had spent weeks imagining moving boxes and frantic apartment searches. The letter arrived on a Tuesday. She opened it at the kitchen counter, skimmed past the legal boilerplate, and found the line: the building was updating its pet policy and removing weight restrictions entirely. Rosalind made a sound that was half laugh, half sob, and Biscuit, hearing it, came thundering across the apartment to investigate. She dropped to her knees on the linoleum and wrapped both arms around his enormous neck while he licked her ear. "We're staying, buddy," she kept telling him. "You big lump, we're staying." She signed the renewal immediately, then took him on a long walk to the park they both adored, letting him sniff every single tree without once tugging the leash, buying herself an ice cream and him a plain vanilla cone from the cart.

The letter from the landlord was two lines long: my security deposit, the one I had written off years ago after the bathtub flood that wasn't my fault, was being returned in full with interest, because an insurance claim had finally settled. There was a check stapled to it. I stood in the doorway of my apartment doing math on my fingers like a child. It was enough for the flight home to Manila, the one I had been putting off for three Christmases because of money. I sat on the floor with my back against the door and called my lola, and when she picked up I could barely talk, I was laughing so much. She thought something terrible had happened. Then I told her, and she shrieked, and I heard her shouting the news to my aunt in the kitchen. I booked the ticket that night, still on the floor, and then lay on the rug looking at the confirmation email, scrolling up and down, reading my own name on it over and over.

The board flipped to DELAYED, and the whole gate groaned in unison. Except Ingrid, who let out a tiny squeak and pressed her hand over her mouth. Her flight to Oslo pushed back three hours meant that her brother, whose connecting flight from Chicago had been running late, would now land in time to fly with her. They had not traveled together since they were teenagers. She texted him in all capitals, then paced to the window and back, unable to sit, watching the planes taxi as if one of them might be his. When he finally appeared at the end of the concourse, rumpled and carrying a ridiculous neck pillow shaped like a shark, she ran. Actually ran, dodging rolling suitcases, and crashed into him so hard he dropped the pillow. They bought terrible airport pretzels and sat on the floor by an outlet sharing earbuds, the way they had on long car trips as kids, and every time the gate agent announced another small delay, Ingrid just grinned and settled in closer.

My flight was delayed six hours, and I'm not going to pretend I wasn't annoyed for the first twenty minutes. But then I wandered into the little terminal bookshop and found, on the clearance shelf, a hardcover edition of a novel I had been hunting for since college, the one my grandfather used to read aloud. Signed. Three dollars. I actually laughed out loud, and the cashier gave me a look. I took it to a quiet corner by the window where the afternoon light was coming in gold and slanted, propped my feet on my carry-on, and started reading. Within ten pages I could hear his voice in my head, the way he did the accents. Every so often I looked up at the runway and caught myself smiling at nothing. A little boy across the aisle was watching me, and when I winked at him he hid behind his mother, giggling. By the time they called boarding I'd read half the book, and I was almost sorry to have to close it and get on the plane.

Jun Watanabe had flown more than two hundred times for work, so a four-hour delay in Denver barely registered. What registered was the snow. Real snow, thick flakes drifting past the tall terminal windows, the first he had seen in the eleven years since he moved to Singapore. He pressed his palm flat against the cold glass. Around him, travelers muttered and argued with gate agents, but Jun felt something unclench in his chest, a boyish lightness he hadn't felt since his childhood winters in Sapporo. He bought a hot chocolate, which he hadn't done in years either, with extra whipped cream, and stood at the window drinking it, watching the ground crews in their orange vests trudging through the white. He photographed the flakes landing on the wing of a parked plane and sent it to his sister with the message, remember this? She replied with a string of snowman emojis. Jun laughed quietly, wrapped both hands around the warm cup, and hoped, a little guiltily, that the delay would last just a bit longer.

We were stuck at gate B14 for what turned into the whole night, and it was the best night of my trip. It started when a woman with a guitar case asked the gate agent if anyone would mind music. Nobody minded. She played, and then a man in a business suit pulled a harmonica out of his briefcase, of all places, and joined her. Somebody's grandmother started clapping on the off-beat. I'm not a singer, but by midnight I was belting out an old Fleetwood Mac song with thirty strangers, my voice cracking, tears in my eyes from laughing so hard. A pilot walked by, stopped, and sang the chorus with us before heading to his own gate. The vending machine ran out of chips and nobody cared. I traded phone numbers with a nursing student from Ghana named Abena and a retired fisherman from Maine. When our plane finally boarded at dawn, people hugged at the jet bridge. I slept the whole flight with a smile stuck on my face.

Lucía was nine and had never been in an airport before, so when the screen said her family's flight was delayed, she didn't understand why her father sighed. More airport meant more moving walkways. She rode them up and down, arms spread out like wings, while her mother watched from a bench, shaking her head but smiling. She discovered that the windows by gate C2 looked right at the planes being refueled, and she knelt there with her nose against the glass, naming the colors of each airline's tail. A flight attendant passing by noticed her and came back a few minutes later with a pair of plastic pilot wings, pinning them on Lucía's sweatshirt. Lucía stood up very straight and saluted. She spent the next hour explaining to every person who would listen that she was now an official pilot. When her father finally said it was time to board, she groaned, then grabbed his hand and pulled him toward the gate, skipping, her new wings bouncing on her chest.

The delay meant I would miss the morning meeting in Toronto, and when the gate agent announced it I felt a rush of relief so warm it was almost embarrassing. I hadn't wanted to go. I'd been stretched thin for months. So I called my manager, who told me to just join remotely tomorrow, and suddenly I had an entire unscheduled afternoon in an airport. I found the quiet lounge at the end of the terminal, the one with the big leather chairs, and sank into one with a sigh that came all the way up from my feet. I ordered a bowl of ramen from the noodle counter and ate it slowly, slurping, savoring every bite. I texted my daughter a picture of the noodles and she sent back a GIF of a dancing cat. I read three chapters of a mystery. I called an old college friend just to chat and we talked for forty minutes, laughing about nothing. When I finally boarded that evening, I realized my shoulders had dropped about two inches and I was humming.

Dr. Okafor didn't even sit down. She came through the door already smiling and said, "Clean. The scan is completely clean, Margaret." Margaret Lindqvist, sixty-one, who had been gripping the edge of the paper-covered exam table for twenty minutes, felt her whole body go loose. She laughed, a high, wobbly sound, and then she was crying and laughing at once, and the doctor handed her a tissue and squeezed her shoulder. Out in the parking lot, Margaret sat in her car and didn't start the engine. She rolled the windows down and let the spring air in, smelling cut grass and somebody's barbecue. She called her husband and said only the one word, "Clean," and heard him whoop so loudly she had to hold the phone away from her ear. On the drive home she stopped at the bakery and bought a ridiculous strawberry cake with whipped cream roses, the kind she normally said was too sweet, and she sang along to the radio the whole way, every word, wrong lyrics and all.

The nurse called with the blood test results while I was in line at the hardware store. My iron levels were finally normal. After eighteen months of exhaustion, of falling asleep at my desk and needing a nap after climbing the stairs, the infusions had worked. I said thank you about six times and hung up and just stood there holding a box of wood screws, smiling at the paint swatches. The guy behind me asked if I was all right. I told him I was more than all right, and he laughed and said, "Well, good for you," without knowing what for. I went home and did something I hadn't done in a year and a half: I went for a run. Not far, just around the block twice, but my legs carried me and my lungs didn't burn, and I kept laughing out loud between breaths like a lunatic. A neighbor waved from her porch and I waved back with both arms. That night I signed up for a 5K in October and printed out the confirmation and stuck it on the fridge.

Amara and Kofi had been trying for three years. When the clinic's number lit up her phone, Amara put it on speaker and set it on the kitchen table between them, and they both stared at it as if it might bite. The nurse said, "Your hCG levels are strongly positive. Congratulations." Kofi stood up so fast his chair fell over backward with a crash. Amara covered her face with both hands, and her shoulders shook, and when she lowered them she was beaming so wide her cheeks ached. The nurse was still talking about the next appointment, and Kofi grabbed a pen and wrote the date on his own palm because he couldn't find paper. Then he scooped Amara out of her chair and spun her in a slow circle around the kitchen, careful, so careful, and she laughed into his shoulder. They didn't call anyone yet. They sat on the floor against the cabinets, holding hands, saying names to each other, trying them out loud one at a time, and giggling at the worst ones.

I'm a big man and I've always been told I'd have trouble with my heart, like my father and his father. So when the cardiologist turned his monitor toward me and pointed at the stress test numbers and said, "Mr. Delacroix, your heart is in better shape than mine," I didn't believe him at first. I asked him to say it again. He did, and he grinned, and I let out a laugh that boomed off the little exam room walls. All those mornings at the pool, all those salads my wife made me eat without complaint, well, with some complaint. They had counted. I walked out of that office with a spring in my step I hadn't felt since I was forty. I called my wife from the elevator and told her she was a genius. In the lobby I passed the gift shop and, without thinking, bought her a bouquet of sunflowers, the biggest ones they had, and carried them out to the car grinning at every stranger I passed, and most of them grinned right back at me.

Seven-year-old Theo had been told the allergy test was just a lot of little pokes, and it was, and he had been very brave about it. Now the allergist, Dr. Brennan, crouched down to his eye level and told him the best news: he was not allergic to dogs anymore. He had outgrown it. Theo's mouth fell open. He looked at his mother, who was already pressing her fingers to her lips, eyes shining. "So we can get one?" he whispered. His mother nodded. Theo leapt off the chair and threw his arms around the doctor's knees, then around his mother's waist, then did three laps of the small exam room with his arms out like an airplane, making engine noises. Dr. Brennan laughed and handed him a sticker shaped like a golden retriever, which Theo stuck carefully on his forehead. In the car he talked nonstop the whole way home, listing possible names, changing his mind every block: Pancake, Rocket, Professor, Noodle, Thunder, and finally, triumphantly, Pancake again.

The biopsy results came through the patient portal at 6:14 in the morning, before anyone had called, and I read the word benign on my phone while still lying in bed. I read it four times. Then I put the phone face-down on the blanket and lay there with my eyes on the ceiling, feeling my heartbeat slow and my breath go all the way down into my belly for the first time in nine days. The window was cracking blue at the edges. A bird started up outside. I got up and made pancakes, which I never do on a weekday, the kind with blueberries, and I made too many and didn't care. When my roommate Sanjana stumbled in, half asleep, I handed her a plate and told her, and she dropped her fork and hugged me so hard I nearly lost my balance. We ate standing at the counter, sticky syrup everywhere, laughing about the stupid worst-case scenarios we had both secretly been imagining all week. I went to work late, still humming.

Mr. Galloway walked down the rows handing back the chemistry exams face down, and Nadia kept her hands flat on the desk so they wouldn't shake. She had failed the midterm. She had spent every lunch period since then in his classroom, working problems until her pencil wore down to a nub. The paper landed in front of her. She flipped the corner up. A ninety-four, circled in red, and beneath it in his tiny handwriting: See what happens? Nadia's breath caught. She slapped her hand over her mouth so she wouldn't shriek in the middle of class, but her feet drummed on the floor under the desk anyway. Her friend Corinne leaned over and saw it and mouthed a silent scream. When the bell rang Nadia went straight to his desk and couldn't think of anything to say, so she just held the test up and grinned, and he grinned back and gave her a little nod. In the hallway she called her mom, and her voice kept cracking into laughter between words.

I'm forty-four and I went back to community college to finish the degree I abandoned when my son was born. My first test was in statistics, the subject I'd been most frightened of. When the professor handed it back, I didn't look at the grade right away; I folded it in half and put it in my bag and didn't look until I got out to my car. An A-minus. I sat in the parking lot with the engine off and read every comment in the margins, every little checkmark. "Excellent reasoning." "Very clear." I hadn't had anyone write something like that about my thinking since I was eighteen. I laughed out loud alone in my car, and then I took a picture of it and sent it to my son, who is in his own second year of university now. He called back within a minute and said, "Mom, are you kidding me? That's better than my stats grade." I'm not ashamed to say I stuck that test on the refrigerator with a magnet, right where his drawings used to go.

Ravi had written his history essay on the 1857 rebellion, using letters his great-great-grandfather had written that his family kept in a tin box. Ms. Achterberg handed it back and asked him to stay after class. His stomach dropped; he was sure he'd broken some rule about sources. Instead, she tapped the top of the page, where she had written a full A and the words, Would your family allow this to be submitted to the state history competition? Ravi stared at her. Then he started talking very fast, explaining the letters, his grandmother's stories, how the ink had faded on one page. She listened, nodding, smiling at his rush of words. He walked out of the classroom and down the hallway practically floating, the essay held against his chest in both arms. At home he burst through the door shouting for his grandmother, who was at the stove, and when he showed her, she wiped her hands on her apron and held the paper at arm's length and began, very quietly, to beam.

Our art teacher, Mr. Fujimoto, gave back the final portfolio reviews on the last day before winter break. I'd taken a risk with mine, painting my abuela's hands in close-up, every wrinkle and vein, instead of a nice safe landscape. He laid the critique sheet on my table and moved on without a word, which made my pulse jump. I turned it over. He had written only two sentences: These hands are alive. You are an artist, Gabriela. I read it, and the room went kind of soft and blurry, and I had to blink fast. I didn't care about the letter grade at the bottom. I folded the paper very carefully along its old creases and slid it inside my sketchbook. On the bus home I kept opening the sketchbook just to peek at it, and every time, a little fizz went up through my ribs. That evening I showed abuela the painting and the note, and she held her own hands up next to the canvas and laughed and laughed, comparing them, saying I had made her look far too pretty.

The physics final had been brutal, and Sebastian was certain he had bombed the last problem, the one about the pendulum. When Professor Lunde started returning papers, he slumped low in his seat, already composing the email to his advisor. His exam landed on the desk. Eighty-eight. And next to the pendulum problem, in green ink: Novel approach, full credit. Better than my solution. Sebastian read it twice, then looked up, and the professor caught his eye from across the lecture hall and lifted his eyebrows as if to say, yes, really. Sebastian felt heat flood his whole face. He pressed his lips together hard to keep from grinning, failed completely, and ended up grinning so wide his ears moved. His lab partner, Ayşe, elbowed him and whispered, "What? What?" and he just slid the paper over to her. She read it and punched his shoulder, laughing. After class they went to the café across the street and he bought both of them the most expensive drink on the menu, something with caramel and too much foam.

My spelling test came back with a gold star on it, the big kind that Mrs. Patterson only gives for a hundred percent, and I had never got one before, not even once, not in the whole year. I'm dyslexic, and spelling is the worst thing, worse than math. But Mum and I had practiced every night at the kitchen table with the magnet letters, even when I cried and wanted to quit. When I saw the star I couldn't sit still. My legs kept bouncing and I kept touching it to feel the crinkly edges. At recess I showed it to my friend Oluwaseun and he said it was the shiniest star he'd ever seen, and we took turns holding it up to the sun to see it sparkle. After school I ran out the gate so fast my backpack bumped against my back, and when I saw Mum waiting I held the paper up over my head and shouted, and she dropped her umbrella right in a puddle and ran to meet me halfway.

Wanjiru was squeezing avocados in the produce aisle when she heard a laugh she would have known anywhere, a goofy honk that ended in a snort. She spun around. Three bins over, by the mangoes, stood Clementine Dubois, her college roommate, whom she hadn't seen in fourteen years. Wanjiru dropped the avocado. It rolled under the display and neither of them cared. "Clem!" she shouted, and half the store turned to look. Clementine whirled, saw her, and let out the honk again, louder, and then they were hugging in the middle of the aisle, rocking side to side, blocking a man with a cart who waited patiently and eventually smiled. They talked right there for forty minutes, leaning on Clementine's cart, interrupting each other, finishing each other's stories about that disastrous road trip to Montreal. Wanjiru's ice cream melted in her basket. Neither of them noticed until a stock boy politely pointed at the puddle. They exchanged numbers, then decided that wasn't enough and made plans for dinner that very night.

I was reaching for the last box of the good cereal when another hand grabbed it at the same moment. I looked up ready to be polite and give it up, and there was Arturo, my best friend from Little League, the kid who had taught me to throw a curveball behind the dugout when we were ten. He had a beard now and a toddler in the cart seat, but the gap in his front teeth was exactly the same. We both said each other's names at the same time and then just stood there laughing, both still holding the cereal box. His daughter looked from him to me, very suspicious. I told her I used to be her dad's catcher, and Arturo said I used to be the worst catcher in the county, and I punched him in the shoulder like we were eleven. We ended up walking the rest of the store together, filling each other in, his wife, my divorce, his job, my new dog. At the checkout he let me have the cereal. I told him I'd trade it for a game of catch on Sunday, and he shook on it.

Mrs. Henrietta Bloom, eighty-two, had been leaning on her cart in the bakery section trying to decide between rye and sourdough when someone said, "Etta? Etta Bloom?" She turned slowly. A tiny woman in a purple raincoat was staring at her, mouth open. It took Henrietta a long moment, and then she saw it in the eyes: Rosa Feldman, who had sat beside her at the switchboard of the telephone company in 1961. Henrietta's hand flew to her chest. "Rosie!" They reached for each other across the carts and held on, both of them trembling a little, laughing in thin high voices. Rosa said she had moved back to town to live with her grandson. Henrietta said she lived just four blocks from here. They stared at each other in wonder. A young clerk came over to ask if they needed help and ended up taking their picture with Rosa's phone, the two of them pressed cheek to cheek, grinning. Henrietta forgot the bread entirely. She walked out with Rosa's address written on her receipt, holding it like a winning ticket.

The checkout line was long and I was tired, staring at the tabloids, when the cashier said, "Oh my God. Is that Ziggy?" Nobody has called me Ziggy since high school. I looked up and it was Lorraine Mbeki, my lab partner from junior year, the girl who set our table on fire during the Bunsen burner unit and then laughed so hard she couldn't put it out. She was wearing a name tag that said ASSISTANT MANAGER. I started laughing before I could say anything, and so did she, and the people in line behind me shifted around trying to figure out what was going on. She rang me up in slow motion so we could talk. She has three kids. I have a cat. She asked if I still played the trumpet, and I admitted I did, badly, in a community band, and she clapped her hands and said she was coming to the next concert. She bagged my groceries herself, very carefully, putting the eggs on top, and tucked a free chocolate bar in the bag with a wink. I ate it in the car, grinning, before I'd even pulled out.

Hamid had been away from Kabul for twenty years, and in this suburban grocery store in Virginia, he had never once heard his own dialect spoken. So when a voice behind him at the spice shelf said, in perfect Dari, that the cardamom here was always stale, he froze. He turned around. The man was gray-haired, heavier, but his face rearranged itself in Hamid's memory into the boy who had lived across the courtyard, the boy he had flown kites with on Fridays. "Jawad?" The man's eyes went wide. Then they were embracing, thumping each other's backs, both talking at once, switching between Dari and English and back again. Shoppers steered around them. Jawad was laughing, wiping his eyes with the back of his hand, saying he knew a shop across town that had real cardamom, real saffron, real everything. Hamid put down his basket right there in the aisle. They walked out together into the bright parking lot, still talking, and drove off in Jawad's car to find that shop and to have tea.

Sinéad was reading the label on a jar of pickles, deciding whether she could justify the expensive ones, when she felt a tap on her shoulder and turned to find Beatrix grinning at her. Beatrix, who had moved to Australia eight years ago and stopped answering emails. Beatrix, who had been her bridesmaid. Sinéad nearly dropped the pickles. "You're back?" she squeaked. Beatrix nodded, eyes sparkling, and said she'd only landed on Tuesday and had been working up the nerve to call. Sinéad set the jar down and grabbed both her hands and squeezed them, bouncing slightly on her toes the way she had when they were twenty. They didn't bother finishing their shopping. They abandoned their carts by the deli counter with a hasty apology to the clerk and went next door to the little café, where they ordered two slices of carrot cake and sat for three hours. When the café closed, they were still talking on the sidewalk, and Sinéad couldn't stop reaching over to touch Beatrix's arm, as if to make sure she was really there.

The car shuddered, coughed, and rolled to a stop on the shoulder of Route 9, and Desmond Achebe sat with his hands on the wheel and started, very slowly, to smile. He was supposed to be presenting the quarterly numbers at nine. He had been dreading it for a week. Now it was 8:20, he was in the middle of nowhere, and there was nothing whatsoever he could do. He called the office, explained, and heard his boss say not to worry, they'd push it to Thursday. Desmond hung up and leaned back in the seat. Then he got out. The morning was cool and clear, mist lifting off a field of corn on the other side of the guardrail. A red-winged blackbird trilled from a fence post. He hadn't been outside at this hour without rushing in years. He sat on the hood of his car, which was still warm, and ate the banana from his bag, watching the mist burn off. When the tow truck finally arrived an hour later, the driver found him whistling.

My old Volvo died on the hill right outside the elementary school, steam hissing out from under the hood, and I was ready to swear when I noticed that the car had stopped directly in front of a bakery I had never seen before. Small, yellow awning, a chalkboard sign that said FRESH CARDAMOM BUNS. I laughed out loud alone in my car. I called the tow company, who said ninety minutes, and then I went inside. The smell hit me like a warm blanket. The owner, an older Swedish woman named Solveig, put a bun on a plate and wouldn't let me pay when she heard my car had broken down outside. I sat by the window with a coffee and watched the school kids lining up for the bell, waving to their parents. The bun was perfect, flaky and sticky and fragrant. I ate it slowly, licking sugar off my thumb. Solveig came over to chat, and by the time the tow truck arrived, I had promised to come back every Saturday, and I meant it.

Valentina's car gave out at a red light, two miles from the hospital where she worked as a nurse. She banged the steering wheel once, then twice, and was digging for her phone when someone knocked on the window. It was a teenage boy in a hoodie, and behind him, four more kids with backpacks. "We can push you," he said. "There's a lot right there." Before she could answer, they were behind the car, grunting and laughing, sneakers slipping on the asphalt, and she steered while they shoved her into a gas station lot. They cheered when it rolled to a stop. Valentina got out laughing, her bad mood evaporated completely. She tried to give them money and they refused, so she ran into the gas station and bought five of the biggest sodas they had and a bag of donuts, and they all stood around in the lot eating and talking about their science teacher. When her husband pulled in to get her, she was still chuckling, and she waved at the boys from his car until they were out of sight.

I'm a mechanic, so when my own truck broke down on the way to work, I'll admit it was a little funny. Fuel pump, I could tell from the sound. I pulled onto a side street and popped the hood, and a little girl on a front porch across the road watched me with enormous curiosity. Her grandfather came out, an old guy in suspenders, and asked if I needed a hand. Turned out he'd been a mechanic for forty years before he retired, and he still had a full garage behind the house. Within twenty minutes we had the truck in his driveway and were both up to our elbows in it, swapping stories about the worst engines we had ever seen. His granddaughter, Meenal, brought us lemonade and handed me tools like a surgical nurse. I couldn't stop grinning. I was two hours late to my own shop, and I didn't care in the slightest. When I finally drove off, the old man and Priya waved from the porch, and I honked the horn twice, like a kid.

When the engine died on the bridge, Callum's first emotion was annoyance. His second, when he got out and looked over the railing, was something else entirely. Below him the river was full of rowing crews, eight boats gliding in the early light, the oars rising and falling in perfect unison, the coxswains' voices floating up thin and clear. Callum had rowed in university, twenty years and thirty pounds ago. He leaned on the cold railing, transfixed, while traffic crept past his hazard lights. One crew started a sprint and he found himself muttering the old rhythm under his breath, drive, catch, drive, catch, his own shoulders twitching along. A cyclist stopped beside him to watch too. "Gorgeous, isn't it," she said, and he agreed with a grin that took over his whole face. By the time the tow truck came, he had looked up the local masters rowing club on his phone and sent them an email asking about beginner sessions. He hummed in the tow truck cab all the way to the garage.

The car broke down at the end of my street, barely a block from my apartment, and I sat there laughing at the absurdity before calling in. My manager, Ines, told me to take the day off; she said I had more than enough personal time and it was about time I used some. I walked home in the sunshine, swinging my laptop bag, and the whole world looked different at nine in the morning on a Wednesday. The coffee shop on the corner was quiet. Old men played dominoes outside the barbershop and one of them nodded to me. I called a garage, arranged the tow, then changed into shorts and went to the park with a book. I ended up lying on my back on the grass, watching clouds, which I hadn't done since I was a child. A dog came over and sniffed my face, and its owner apologized, and I told her it was the best thing that had happened to me all week. Which was true, I thought, stretching, until the car breaking down.

It was 11:40 when Graciela heard the key in the lock, and she set down her crossword and listened. Her son Mateo came in quietly, the way he always did, but then he saw the light on in the living room and practically bounded over to her. "Mamá, you're still up? Good. I have to tell you." He dropped onto the couch beside her and the whole cushion bounced. The girl he had been too shy to talk to for a whole semester, Daniela, had asked him to dance at the school formal. Then she had asked him to dance again. Then they had talked for two hours on the steps outside. Graciela watched his face as he talked, lit up and animated, his hands flying, and felt something swell warm in her chest. She hadn't seen him this talkative since he was nine. She made him hot chocolate though it was nearly midnight, and they sat together with their mugs while he told her every detail, and she laughed at all the right places and some of the wrong ones.

I was waiting up for my daughter, sitting in the dark kitchen like my own mother used to, when headlights swept across the window at exactly 10:59. One minute before curfew. For months it had been fights about curfew, slammed doors, sullen silence, and I had braced myself for another one. But Ayesha came in and, before she even took off her shoes, she came over and hugged me. Just like that, unprompted, arms around my neck. "Thanks for letting me go," she said into my shoulder. I couldn't answer for a moment. There was a lump in my throat and a grin trying to break out across my face at the same time. She pulled back and started telling me about the concert, the band, how the drummer threw a stick into the crowd and her friend caught it. I put the kettle on, and we sat at the table, and she talked and I listened, and when she finally went up to bed I stayed in the kitchen alone a while longer, smiling into my cooling tea.

Leopold had been waiting up for his son since ten o'clock, pretending to read, when the front door burst open at eleven and Finn came in shouting. "Dad! Dad, they called back!" Leopold leaped up so fast the book went flying. Finn, seventeen and six-foot-two, was waving his phone like a flag. The drama club director had called while Finn was at the cast party for the spring play: a scout from the summer theater program in Chicago had been in the audience, and they were offering Finn a full scholarship. Leopold felt something huge break open in his chest. He grabbed his son by the shoulders, then pulled him into a bear hug, and the two of them stumbled around the living room in a kind of clumsy dance, knocking a lamp askew. Finn's mother came down the stairs in her bathrobe to see what was going on and then joined in. They didn't go to bed until two. They ate cold leftover pizza at the kitchen table, and Leopold kept clapping Finn on the back for no reason at all.

The clock said 12:15 and I was on the sofa in my robe when I heard the car door and then laughter, two voices, one of them my son's. I went to the window. Kwame and his friend Nkosi were standing in the driveway in the porch light, doubled over, and Nkosi's mother waved from her car before pulling away. When Kwame came in he was flushed and grinning and couldn't explain what was funny because every time he tried, he started laughing again. Something about a goat at the county fair. It was contagious. I hadn't even heard the story and I was already wheezing, holding the back of a chair. Since his father moved out last spring, he had barely smiled at all, and I had spent so many nights sitting up worrying about him. Now here he was in my hallway, red-faced, tears of laughter running down his cheeks, trying to do an impression of the goat. I made him tell it three times. By the third time, I was the one who couldn't breathe.

Brigitte had told herself she would not wait up. Her daughter Elodie was nineteen, home from university for the summer, and old enough to come back whenever she liked. Still, Brigitte found herself on the window seat at midnight with a cup of chamomile, watching the street. When Elodie finally came up the path at half past twelve, she wasn't alone. A young woman was walking with her, and at the door they paused, and Elodie kissed her, quickly and shyly, before the young woman headed back toward the bus stop. Elodie came inside and saw her mother on the window seat and froze. Brigitte set down her cup and opened her arms. Elodie crossed the room in three steps and fell into them. "Her name is Mireille," she said, muffled, and Brigitte laughed softly and said she wanted to hear absolutely everything. They talked until the birds started up outside, curled together on the window seat under a blanket, and Brigitte could not remember the last time she had felt so light.

I always wait up. My husband says it's pointless, that Jasper is sixteen and fine, but I can't sleep until I hear the door. Tonight it opened at 11:30 and Jasper came in with grease on his hands and a stupid enormous grin. He'd been at his friend's house fixing up an old motorcycle for three months, and tonight, he informed me, it started. First try. He played me a video on his phone of the engine roaring, and the boys whooping in the background, and I watched his face instead of the screen. He was shining. This kid who had struggled so badly in school, who thought he was dumb, had built something that worked. I told him I wanted to see it in person tomorrow and he said, "Seriously?" with such an eager look that I nearly teared up. I made him wash his hands, and then I made us both grilled cheese sandwiches at midnight, and we ate them at the counter while he explained carburetors to me in great detail. I understood nothing and enjoyed every word.

When her manager called her in, Yuki Tanaka smoothed her blouse in the hallway and walked in with her notebook ready, expecting another project. Instead, Mr. Ellison was standing, and there were three other people in his office, and on the desk was a small cake with candles. "Ten years today," he said. Yuki had completely forgotten. Her hands flew to her cheeks. Her colleagues from the design team started singing, badly and off-key, and she laughed so hard she had to lean against the filing cabinet. Then Mr. Ellison handed her an envelope; inside was a card signed by the whole department, and a voucher for a weekend at a hot spring resort in the mountains. She looked up at all of them, her eyes stinging, and could only say thank you, thank you, over and over. They cut the cake with a plastic knife. Yuki got frosting on her sleeve and didn't even mind. Back at her desk she kept glancing at the card, rereading the little messages, chuckling at the silly drawings people had added in the margins.

"Shut the door, Omar," my manager said, and my stomach dropped. Shut the door is never good. I sat down in the chair across from her and folded my hands so she wouldn't see them fidgeting. Renata looked at me for a moment, then slid a single sheet across the desk. It was an org chart. My name was in a box at the top of a new team. "We want you to lead it," she said. "The client specifically asked for you." I stared at the box with my name in it. My heart was pounding so loudly I was sure she could hear it, but it wasn't fear anymore. A grin was spreading across my face that I couldn't control even a little. I said yes before she finished explaining the salary, then made her repeat the salary, then said yes again. She laughed. When I walked out of her office I went straight to the stairwell, where no one could see, and did a fist pump so hard I almost hit the wall. Then I called my wife and whispered the news like a secret.

Eduardo Salgado had been a line cook at the restaurant for six years, and the head chef had never once called him into the office. When it finally happened on a slow Tuesday, he wiped his hands on his apron twice on the way back. Chef Moreau was sitting at the cluttered little desk with a menu draft in front of her. She turned it around. Under the entrées, in bold, was a new dish: Eduardo's Mole Negro. His grandmother's recipe, the one he made for family meal every Sunday. "The staff won't shut up about it," Moreau said, smiling. "It goes on the menu next week. With your name." Eduardo stood there with his mouth open. Then he laughed, a startled bark, and covered his face with his hands. When he lowered them he was grinning so hard his eyes had nearly disappeared. He went back into the kitchen and the whole line was waiting, because of course they already knew. They banged their spoons on the steel counters until Moreau yelled at them to get back to work.

My manager, Mr. Harrington, called me into his office on my last week before maternity leave, and I waddled in, eight months along, wondering what I'd forgotten to hand over. He had a gift bag on his desk. Inside was a tiny onesie with our company logo on it, which made me snort, and under that, a folded letter. The company was extending paid parental leave from twelve weeks to six months, effective immediately, and he had pushed for it to apply to me. I read it standing up, then had to sit down. The baby kicked, hard, as if she knew. I put my hand on my belly and laughed, and then my eyes filled up, and then I was laughing and crying at once while my poor manager looked around in alarm for tissues. "Good tears," I told him. "These are good tears." He let out a breath and grinned. I walked back to my desk, rubbing my stomach, and spent the rest of the afternoon imagining long mornings at home, the baby asleep on my chest.

Thandiwe had been at the warehouse for only three months when the floor supervisor waved her into the glass-walled office. Through the window, she could see her coworkers watching. She sat stiffly. Mr. Kowalczyk, a big bearded man with reading glasses perched on his head, held up a printout. "Your safety suggestion," he said. "The thing with the loading dock mirrors." She nodded, bracing. "Corporate is rolling it out to all forty-two locations. They want to give you a bonus. And they want you on the safety committee." Thandiwe blinked at him. She had scribbled that idea on a napkin during her lunch break. She started to laugh, and it came out as a surprised giggle that she couldn't stop, her shoulders shaking. Mr. Kowalczyk laughed too, a deep rumble. When she stepped back out onto the floor, her coworkers erupted into applause, a forklift driver honked his horn, and Thandiwe gave a little bow, her face burning bright, her whole body tingling.

When the email said my manager wanted to see me at four, I spent the afternoon guessing. Layoffs? A complaint? But Dariusz just smiled when I sat down and asked me how my mother was doing. She'd had a stroke in the spring, and I'd been driving four hours every weekend to see her. I told him she was getting better slowly. He nodded and said, "How would you feel about working from Ohio? Permanently. Fully remote." I just sat there. For months I'd been calculating whether I could afford to quit, whether I could find work near her. He watched me and his smile got wider. "I'll take that as a yes," he said. I managed to nod. Then words came tumbling out, thank you, are you sure, thank you, and I think I reached across the desk and shook his hand three separate times. When I left the building, I sat in my car and called my mother. Her speech is still slow, but when she understood, she made a sound I will remember for the rest of my life, a long, wobbly, bubbling laugh.

The attic was stifling, and Lena had been sneezing through boxes of tax records for an hour when she found the shoebox labeled FAN MAIL in her late father's blocky handwriting. Fan mail? Her father had been an accountant. She opened it. Inside were dozens of envelopes, all addressed to him, all from the same person: her. Every letter she'd written from summer camp, every postcard from her semester in Spain, every birthday card she had drawn as a kid with crayon suns and stick-figure dogs. He'd kept them all, in order, with the dates penciled on the back. Lena sat down right there on the dusty floorboards. She pulled out a card she must have made at five: a lopsided purple heart and the words BEST DAD IN THE GALAXY. She laughed so suddenly that dust puffed up off the box. She spent the rest of the afternoon reading them, one by one, giggling at her terrible spelling and her dramatic camp complaints, her face warm, sunlight slanting in through the small round window.

I was clearing out the attic before we sold the house when I found a letter tucked inside an old copy of Jane Eyre. It was addressed to me, in my wife's handwriting, dated forty-one years ago, the week before our wedding. I didn't know it existed. Clara must have written it and lost it, or meant to give it to me and forgot. I sat down on a trunk and unfolded it carefully. She listed all the reasons she was marrying me, numbered one through twenty. Number seven was that I sing badly but loudly. Number fourteen was that I once drove three hours to bring her soup when she had the flu. Number twenty just said, Because you make me laugh every single day. I was laughing before I got to the end, wiping my eyes with my sleeve. I went downstairs, where Clara was wrapping dishes in newspaper, and handed it to her without a word. She read it, put her hand over her mouth, and then started laughing too, and said she'd been looking for that for forty years.

Dmitri was hauling a box of Christmas decorations down from the attic of his grandparents' farmhouse when the bottom gave out and a flood of tinsel and old papers spilled over the stairs. Among them was a yellowed envelope with a stamp he didn't recognize, Soviet, from 1972. He opened it on the landing. It was a letter from a woman named Galina to his grandfather, written in Russian, and Dmitri's Russian was rusty, but he worked through it slowly, mouthing the words. She was writing to say she accepted his proposal. That she would come to America. That she was not afraid. Dmitri's grandmother was Galina. He'd never heard this story; she had always just said they met at a dance. He went downstairs, waving the letter, and found her in the kitchen rolling dough. When she saw it, she put down the rolling pin and pressed her floury hands to her cheeks, leaving white prints, and started to giggle like a girl. She made him sit at the table, poured two glasses of tea, and told him everything.

There's a trunk in our attic I've avoided for years because it's full of my college junk. Today, looking for my old ice skates, I finally opened it. Under a stack of chemistry notes was a letter I had written to myself in freshman orientation, one of those to be opened in ten years exercises. I had forgotten it completely. It was dated twenty years ago. My eighteen-year-old self had asked: Are you a vet yet? Did you get a dog named Sir Barksalot? Are you still friends with Marguerite? I sat in the dusty light laughing out loud at my own ridiculous handwriting, the hearts dotting the i's. I'm a vet. I have three dogs, none of them named Sir Barksalot, sadly. And Marguerite is my daughter's godmother. I took a picture of the letter and texted it to her, and she called back immediately, howling with laughter, demanding to know where Sir Barksalot was. I told her I'd adopt one this week and name him properly. I'm not entirely sure I was kidding. I kept the letter on my nightstand that night.

Pilar found the letter wedged between two rafters, as if someone had hidden it on purpose. The envelope was addressed to whoever finds this. She glanced around the cramped attic of the old house she'd bought last month, and a grin crept onto her face. Inside, in looping old-fashioned cursive, a girl named Eleanor, age eleven, 1938, had written that she was hiding this letter as a time capsule, and she hoped whoever found it liked the house as much as she did. She said the third stair creaks if you step in the middle. She said the best place to read is the window seat in the back bedroom when it rains. She said there was a loose brick by the fireplace with a surprise behind it. Pilar scrambled down the attic ladder so fast she scraped her shin. She ran to the fireplace, pressed brick after brick, until one wobbled. Behind it was a small tin holding a marble, a hair ribbon, and a buffalo nickel. Pilar sat back on her heels and laughed, giddy beyond words.

The letter was in my grandfather's old army footlocker, folded small, and it was from me. I was seven when I wrote it. He had been in the hospital for his hip, and I had sent him a letter full of urgent questions: Do they give you pudding. Is the bed like a spaceship. Can you come to my birthday. I had forgotten writing it. But he had saved it in the footlocker with his medals and his discharge papers, which told me exactly how much it had mattered to him. On the back, in his shaky handwriting, he had answered every question. Yes, chocolate pudding. Yes, it goes up and down like a spaceship. And: I would not miss your birthday for all the tea in China. I remembered then. He came. He used a walker and he sat on the porch and I made him wear a paper crown. I sat there on the attic floor grinning, the letter in my lap, my chest warm and full, hearing his gravelly laugh as clearly as if he were up there with me.

Giuseppe had the radio turned up loud and was singing along to Dean Martin, badly, as he stirred the risotto with one hand and conducted the orchestra with the wooden spoon in the other. In forty minutes his whole family would be here, all of them, for the first time in six years: his sister from Naples, his brother from Melbourne, the nieces and nephews he only knew from video calls. The kitchen was a glorious mess. Flour on the counter, a pot of ragù murmuring on the back burner, garlic and rosemary so thick in the air he could taste them. He tasted the risotto, closed his eyes, kissed his fingertips like a cartoon chef, and laughed at himself. His wife came in to steal a piece of bread and he grabbed her by the waist and twirled her once around the island, nearly knocking over the olive oil. She swatted him with a dish towel. When the doorbell rang early, he wiped his hands on his apron and ran down the hallway, shouting their names before he even reached the door.

I'd never cooked for more than two people before, and tonight eight of my new coworkers were coming over to my tiny apartment. I should have been stressed. Instead I spent the afternoon practically dancing between the stove and the counter, because for the first time since I moved to this city, I had friends to cook for. I made my mother's jollof rice, the real way, with the smoky crust at the bottom of the pot. I made puff-puff and dusted them with sugar and ate three while they were still too hot, burning my tongue and not caring. I pushed my desk against the wall and borrowed chairs from the neighbor across the hall, who said she'd come too if there were leftovers. I set out mismatched plates. My playlist was blasting Afrobeats and every few minutes I caught myself shimmying while I stirred. When the buzzer finally went off, I checked my reflection in the microwave door, smoothed my shirt, and opened the door with the biggest grin I'd worn in months.

Odile's daughter-in-law was coming to dinner for the very first time, and the old woman had been up since dawn. Now, at six, the lamb was resting under foil, the potatoes were crackling in duck fat, and the apricot tart sat cooling on the windowsill, perfuming the whole house. Odile hummed an old Breton song as she arranged the table. She had pulled out her mother's lace tablecloth, the one only used at Christmas. She lit the candles early just to see how they would look and stood back with her hands clasped under her chin, beaming at the effect. Her son had sounded so nervous on the phone, so eager for the two of them to get along. Odile tasted the sauce, added a pinch of salt, tasted again, and gave a satisfied little nod. When she heard the car in the drive, she untied her apron, patted her hair, and hurried to the door with quick small steps, already reaching out her arms.

Twenty minutes until the guests arrive, and the soufflé has risen. I'm crouched in front of the oven door with my face practically pressed to the glass, watching it climb up over the rim of the dish, golden and puffed and absolutely perfect, and I'm grinning like a kid at an aquarium. Three times I've tried this recipe. Three times it collapsed into a sad cheesy pancake. But tonight, with my college roommates coming over for our annual reunion dinner, it's standing tall. I want to applaud it. I actually do, quietly, a little golf clap in my empty kitchen. My partner, Tobias, wanders in, sees me crouched there, and asks what on earth I'm doing, and I just point. He kneels down beside me and we watch it together for a second in reverent silence, and then he starts laughing and so do I. The doorbell rings. I leap up so quickly I nearly whack my head on the counter, and I yell at Tobias to guard the oven with his life.

Reuben Silverstein was seventy-eight and had cooked a Friday night dinner every week of his adult life, but this one was special. His granddaughter was bringing her fiancé to meet him. The challah, which he had braided that morning, sat glossy and golden on the cutting board. The chicken soup was simmering, the matzo balls floating like little clouds. He had even put on his good cardigan, the one with leather buttons. As he set out the candlesticks, he caught himself whistling, and he couldn't remember the last time he had whistled. His late wife used to say that he only whistled when the world was right. He paused, then smiled to himself and kept whistling. He tasted the soup with the big wooden spoon, nodded, added a little dill. Outside the window he saw a car pull up, and a tall young man climbing out holding flowers, and his granddaughter laughing at something the young man said. Reuben chuckled, straightened his cardigan, and went to throw open the front door.

Haruka had decided to cook her first Thanksgiving dinner for her American friends as a thank you for her first year in Ohio. She had never roasted a turkey. She had watched eleven videos about it. Now the bird sat on the counter, burnished brown, and when she pressed the thermometer in, it read exactly the right number, and she let out a little squeal and bounced on her toes. Her tiny kitchen was crammed with dishes: mashed potatoes, a green bean casserole she had made from a recipe card her neighbor gave her, and, because she couldn't help herself, a big platter of karaage and a pot of miso soup. She thought her friends might find it funny. She hoped they would. The windows were fogged up from all the steam and she drew a smiley face on one with her finger. When the first knock came she was still wearing her oven mitts, and she opened the door with them on, waving both enormous padded hands in greeting, laughing at herself.

The moving truck pulled away, and Esperanza stood in the middle of her new apartment in Chicago surrounded by boxes and silence, and she spun in a slow circle with her arms out. Hardwood floors. A bay window that looked out over a street lined with maple trees, the leaves turning orange. A radiator that clanked comfortingly. After four years of living with her parents in Tucson, saving every paycheck, this was hers. She opened the window and let the cold air in, breathing it deep, smelling woodsmoke and something baking from the café downstairs. She found the box marked KITCHEN and dug out a single mug and the kettle, made tea, and sat on the floor with her back against the wall, just looking at the room. The light was moving across the floorboards. Somebody downstairs was practicing the cello. Esperanza laughed softly to herself for no reason at all, then pulled out her phone and sent her mother a photo of the bay window with nothing but a long row of exclamation points.

I dragged the last box up four flights of stairs, dropped it in the doorway of my new place in Lisbon, and collapsed on the floor laughing, sweaty and out of breath. The apartment is barely bigger than my old bedroom in Manchester. The shower is in the kitchen, basically. But there's a tiny balcony, and from the balcony I can see the river, and red rooftops tumbling down the hill, and a yellow tram rattling around a corner right below me. I stood out there for ten minutes before I unpacked anything. Swallows were cutting through the sky. An old woman on the balcony across the street was hanging laundry and she waved at me. I waved back with both arms like a fool. Then I went downstairs to the little shop on the corner and bought bread, cheese, a bottle of wine, and a custard tart, and I ate all of it sitting cross-legged on the balcony as the sun went down, the whole city glowing orange. I kept saying it out loud to nobody: I live here. I actually live here now.

When Oskar opened the door to his new apartment in Seattle, the first thing he saw was a basket on the kitchen counter. Inside were a loaf of homemade sourdough, a jar of local honey, a bag of coffee beans, and a card: Welcome to the building! We're in 3B. Come say hi! —Mei and Arjun. Oskar set down his duffel bag and read the card twice, a smile spreading slowly over his face. He had moved across the country for a job where he knew nobody, and he had spent the whole drive from Minneapolis worrying that he'd be lonely. He opened the coffee and the rich smell filled the empty room. He didn't even unpack. He washed his face, put on a clean shirt, and went straight down the hall to 3B. Mei opened the door holding a toddler on her hip, and behind her Arjun was cooking something with a lot of ginger. They pulled him inside, and he ended up staying for dinner, laughing at the toddler, who kept offering him soggy crackers, until well past nine o'clock.

My new apartment in Montreal has a claw-foot bathtub. I didn't notice it in the listing photos, so when I walked in with my first armful of boxes and saw it there, white and deep, standing on its little iron feet under a window, I actually shrieked. My brother, who was helping me move, came running in thinking I'd seen a mouse, and found me standing in the empty bathroom with both hands pressed to my face. He started laughing at me, and then I laughed, and we stood there giggling like kids. I've lived in places with only a shower stall for nine years. I love baths more than almost anything. That night, after he'd left and the boxes were still everywhere and I had no idea where my sheets were, I filled that tub to the brim with hot water and a bath bomb I'd bought specially, and sank in up to my chin. Snow was falling outside the window, big slow flakes in the streetlight. I lay there until the water went cool, grinning at the ceiling.

Abdullahi had lived in a refugee camp, then a shelter, then a shared room with four other men. Now, at thirty-two, he stood in a small one-bedroom apartment in Minneapolis, holding a key that was entirely his. The caseworker had left. He walked through each room slowly: the kitchen, with its little gas stove; the bedroom, with a real window; the bathroom, where he turned the faucet on and off three times just to watch the water come. He laughed quietly at himself. He set his single bag on the floor and took out the one thing he had carried through everything, a small woven mat his mother had made, and spread it beneath the window. He sat down on it. The afternoon sun came in warm across his legs. Outside, children were playing on a lawn and someone was grilling meat. He called his sister in Nairobi on a video call and carried the phone around, showing her every corner, and she clapped and cried out at each room, and he grinned until his cheeks ached.

Fiona had moved to Edinburgh on a whim after her divorce, signing a lease on a flat she'd only seen on video, and she spent the whole train ride up from London wondering if she'd lost her mind. Then she climbed the narrow stone stairs, unlocked the door, and found the flat flooded with late-afternoon light. Through the tall sash windows she could see the castle on its rock, gold against a pale sky. She dropped her suitcase with a thump. For a while she just stood there with her coat still on, mouth slightly open. Then she started laughing, a big, loose, unguarded laugh that she hadn't heard come out of herself in two years. She opened the window and leaned out, and somewhere down below a busker was playing the bagpipes, and it was so ridiculous and so perfect that she laughed even harder. She didn't unpack a thing that evening. She went out, found a pub with a fire going, ordered a whisky, and chatted with the bartender for an hour about the city she now got to call home.

Mile twenty-five, and Kenji's legs were made of wet sand, and he was grinning anyway. The crowd along the barricades was so loud he could feel it in his ribs. A woman in a banana costume held out a sign that said YOU'RE ALMOST THERE, STRANGER, and he high-fived her as he passed, laughing. A year ago he couldn't run to the end of his street. He had been forty pounds heavier and couldn't climb stairs without wheezing. Now he was in the final mile of the Boston Marathon, and his body hurt in every possible way, and he loved all of it. The sun was on his face. Kids were holding out orange slices. He grabbed one and bit into it and the juice was the best thing he had ever tasted. When he turned onto Boylston Street and saw the finish line banner, his eyes blurred, and he pumped both fists in the air, and the crowd roared like it was just for him. He crossed the line with his arms spread wide like he was flying.

There's a point in the last mile when your body stops complaining and just runs, and I hit it right as we came around the lake. My feet were blistered, my calves had cramped twice, and I didn't care about any of it. Ahead of me I could hear the drums at the finish, and the announcer reading names. I started laughing, alone, gasping for air, because I had done it. Two years of training through chemo and after chemo. My oncologist had told me I was crazy and then signed up to run with me, and she was somewhere back there behind me, probably cursing my name. A man on the sidewalk was ringing a cowbell and screaming, Go Pooja! because my name was printed on my bib, and I waved at him like we were old friends. My daughters were at the finish holding a giant sign with my face glued onto a superhero body. When I saw it I laughed so hard I almost stopped running. I crossed the line and they nearly knocked me over.

Augustin and his twin sister Céleste had promised each other, when they were nine, that they would run a marathon side by side someday. Now they were fifty-three, gray at the temples, and in the last mile of the Paris Marathon, and Céleste kept bumping his shoulder with hers and giggling. "We are idiots," she panted. "Complete idiots." "The best idiots," Augustin agreed, wheezing. The cobblestones were murder on his knees. A brass band was playing on a street corner, and a crowd of teenagers was dancing to it, and when they saw the twins running in matching neon headbands, they cheered wildly. Céleste blew them kisses. Augustin grabbed her hand without thinking, the way he had when they crossed the street as children, and she squeezed it hard. With four hundred meters to go they both started to sprint, laughing like lunatics, elbows flying, absolutely refusing to let the other one win. They crossed the line at exactly the same moment, collapsed against each other, and stood there swaying and hugging, unable to stop laughing.

Last mile. I could see it on my watch: 25.2. My lungs were raw and my left hip was screaming, but the morning was so beautiful I kept looking around like a tourist. The route ran along the harbor and the water was glittering, sailboats bobbing, gulls wheeling overhead. Spectators lined the seawall with their coffees, yelling encouragement. A little boy held out his hand for a high five and I swerved to give it to him and he shrieked with excitement and turned to tell his dad. I'm not fast. I was never going to win anything. But I had trained every Saturday for a year with the slow group at my running club, the ones who stop for pastries afterward, and there they were, Bogdan and Leticia and the rest, standing at the 26-mile marker in matching ridiculous tutus, screaming my name and banging pots. I started laughing so hard I nearly tripped. Bogdan jumped the barrier and ran the last stretch beside me in his tutu, flapping his arms like a bird.

Hyun-woo was running his first marathon in Seoul, and with one mile left, he knew he was going to beat his own goal by almost twenty minutes. The realization hit him all at once and a whoop burst out of him, so loud that a runner beside him turned and laughed and gave him a thumbs up. His legs felt strangely light now, as though someone had cut weights off his ankles. The cherry trees along the Han River were in full bloom, petals drifting across the course like pink snow, and he caught one on his tongue and laughed again at how silly that was. Volunteers at the last water station were dancing to K-pop blasting from a speaker. He grabbed a cup, missed his mouth entirely, splashed it all over his face, and kept going, dripping and grinning. He thought about his grandmother, who had walked him to school every day and always said he would do something great. When the finish arch appeared, he raised both hands toward the sky and shouted her name.

Imogen was eleven minutes ahead of her personal best and could barely believe it. The last mile of the Chicago Marathon went straight down Michigan Avenue, the skyline towering on her left, the lake shining on her right, and she ran it with her mouth hanging open in a kind of astonished grin. Her watch kept buzzing at every split and every split was faster. Her body, which she had spent so many years being harsh about, was carrying her like it had been waiting all this time to show off. At Roosevelt Road the course went up a short hill, the cruelest little hill in all of Chicago, and instead of dreading it she put her head down and charged up it, laughing out loud. Somebody in the crowd shouted that she was a beast, and she roared back at them. She could see the clock over the finish. She looked down at her own legs, pumping, mud-splattered, strong, and thought, look at you go. She crossed the line with tears and sweat streaming together, still grinning wide.

Rufus hadn't come in from the yard for twenty minutes, so Coretta finally pulled on her boots and went out into the drizzle to see what he was up to. She found him by the back fence, sitting perfectly still and staring at the woodpile. Then she heard it: a tiny mewing. Coretta crouched down and peered into the gap between the logs. Four kittens, no bigger than her hand, huddled together in a nest of dry leaves, and Rufus, her big slobbery Labrador who was afraid of the vacuum, was guarding them. His tail thumped the wet grass when she looked at him. "Oh, you good, good boy," she whispered, her voice going all wobbly and high. She scratched his ears and he leaned his whole weight against her, nearly toppling her into the mud, and she laughed. She ran inside for a towel and a box, came back, and gently gathered up the kittens one by one while Rufus supervised, his nose an inch from her hands, his tail wagging so hard his whole back end swayed.

Biscotti hadn't come back in after her evening business, and I was just stepping out with a flashlight when I heard the neighbor's kids shrieking with laughter over the fence. I peeked over. My elderly basset hound, who usually moves at the speed of a glacier, was in the middle of their yard tearing around in circles, ears flapping, with three children chasing her and a sprinkler going full blast. She had found the loose board in the fence. She had found the sprinkler. And she had clearly found the best night of her life. She was soaked to the skin, mud up to her belly, and she looked twelve years younger. The kids' dad, Tariq, saw me and waved and called out that she could come over any time. I laughed so hard I had to lean against the fence. When I finally called her, she came trotting back through the gap, dripping and panting, her mouth stretched in a big doggy grin, and shook herself all over my legs. I didn't even mind. I toweled her off on the porch, laughing the whole time.

Ezekiel was eight, and it was his job to let Pepper out in the morning and let her back in. This morning, she didn't come back to the door when he called. He went out in his pajamas and slippers and searched the whole backyard, under the deck, behind the shed, calling her name, until he heard a muffled bark from the old rabbit hutch they never used anymore. He opened the little wire door. Pepper was lying on a bed of straw, and curled up against her belly were five tiny wriggling puppies, eyes shut, squeaking. Ezekiel's mouth fell open. He spun around and sprinted toward the house, slippers flying off one after the other, screaming "MOM! DAD! PEPPER HAD BABIES!" so loud that the neighbor's dog started barking. His parents came running out in their bathrobes. They all knelt in the wet grass around the hutch, and Ezekiel's father put an arm around him, and Ezekiel was bouncing so much on his knees that his dad had to hold him still so he wouldn't scare the puppies.

When my dog, Marlowe, didn't come in from the yard, I knew exactly where he was, because it was the first snow of the year and he does this every time. I put on my coat and went out with my coffee. There he was in the middle of the lawn, a black poodle mix in a field of fresh white, rolling on his back with his legs kicking at the sky, snorting with excitement. He saw me and leapt to his feet and did zoomies around the entire yard, plowing through the snow with his face like a little snowplow, snow flying off his ears. I couldn't help it. I set my coffee on the porch rail and went out and scooped up a handful of snow and threw it in the air for him, and he went bananas, leaping and snapping at the flakes. I lost my footing and landed on my backside and he jumped on top of me and licked my face, his whiskers crusted with ice. I lay there in the snow laughing until my ribs hurt, and the coffee went cold on the rail.

Natasha had been calling Hugo for ten minutes, and the old spaniel, who was half deaf now, hadn't come in. She went out the back door and around the side of the house and stopped. Hugo was sitting at the gate, tail sweeping back and forth across the gravel, staring down the road. Then Natasha saw why. A figure in an army uniform was walking up the lane with a duffel bag over his shoulder. Her son. Six months early. Natasha's hand flew to her mouth. Hugo, who had not run in two years, took off down the drive at a stiff, rolling gallop, ears flying, and her son dropped his bag and knelt on the gravel to catch him. Natasha ran too, slippers and all, laughing and crying, and threw her arms around both of them at once. Hugo was whining and licking everybody's faces. "He knew," her son kept saying, laughing. "He knew I was coming." They walked back up to the house together, all three of them, her hand never once letting go of his arm.
