Our beagle, Waffles, hadn't come back in, so I went out to look and found him sitting proudly next to the vegetable bed with something enormous in his mouth. A zucchini. A truly gigantic zucchini, almost as long as he was, which he must have pulled off the vine himself. He was holding it with great dignity, head high, tail going like a metronome, waiting for my approval. I burst out laughing. I'd been trying to grow that thing all summer and had completely missed it under the leaves. "Did you harvest that for me?" I asked him, and he trotted over and dropped it at my feet with a thud and sat down, looking up at me, extremely pleased with himself. I called my husband out to see. He took about thirty photos of Waffles posing with the zucchini, and we were both cackling the whole time. That night I made zucchini bread with it, and Waffles sat by the oven the entire hour it baked, and I gave him a tiny corner of the first slice as his official reward.

Behind the curtain, Ottilie could hear the audience settling in, coughing, rustling programs, the murmur of four hundred voices, and she pressed her forehead against her cello's scroll and smiled. She had played in small cafés and church basements for twelve years. Tonight was the concert hall. Her concert hall, the one she had snuck into as a girl to watch the symphony from the cheap seats. Her fingertips were tingling. She kept flexing them, not from dread but because she couldn't wait to touch the strings. Her accompanist, a lanky young man named Benedikt, came over and gave her a little nudge with his elbow, and they grinned at each other like conspirators. "Ready?" he whispered. "I've been ready since I was seven," she whispered back. The stage manager signaled. Ottilie stood, lifted the cello, and walked out into the warm pool of light. The applause washed over her. She sat, settled the instrument against her chest, closed her eyes, breathed in the smell of rosin and old wood, and began.

Five minutes until we go on, and I'm sitting on an amp in the green room of a dive bar, drumming on my thighs with my sticks, unable to stop smiling. It's our first real show. Not a talent night, not a friend's birthday, a real gig, with a poster on the door and our band's name spelled almost right. The bass player, Szymon, is pacing and stretching his neck. Our singer, Amina, is doing lip trills in the corner, which sounds like a motorboat, and every time she does it I start cracking up and she throws a water bottle at me. Through the door I can hear the crowd getting louder, and someone yells our name, our actual band name, and all four of us freeze and look at each other with huge eyes, and then we all start laughing at once. My heart is going like a kick drum. I've waited for this since I was fourteen, banging on pots in my mom's kitchen. The bartender sticks her head in and says, "You're up." I leap off the amp.

Seventy-year-old Cornelius Abara had played trumpet in a jazz club in Lagos for forty years before he retired and moved to be near his children in Houston. He had not performed since. Tonight, his granddaughter's school had invited him to play at the spring concert, and he stood in the wings of the gymnasium, polishing his horn with a soft cloth for the fifth time, rocking on his heels. He could see the folding chairs, the paper streamers, the parents holding up their phones. His granddaughter, Chiamaka, was in the front row, waving both arms at him like she was guiding in an airplane. Cornelius laughed and waved back. His chest felt wide and warm, the way it used to feel on Saturday nights in the club when the room was full and the band was hot. He wet his lips. He pressed the valves, one, two, three, listening to the familiar click. When the principal said his name into the crackling microphone, he strode out onto the gym floor with a little swing in his hips.

I'm about to play the piano at my best friend's wedding, and I keep peeking out from behind the pillar at the rows of white chairs, at the arch covered in peonies, at Delphine's mother already dabbing her eyes, and I'm so full of fizzing energy I could float up into the rafters. I wrote the piece myself. I've been working on it in secret for eight months. Delphine has no idea. The groom, Marcus, knows, and he keeps catching my eye from the front and grinning and giving me tiny thumbs-ups. The officiant nods at me. I walk to the piano, sit down, crack my knuckles, which makes a little girl in the second row giggle, and I wink at her. Then the back doors open and there's Delphine on her father's arm, and I start to play, and the melody comes out of my hands exactly how I heard it in my head, and Delphine stops walking for a second, realizes, and looks over at me with her mouth open, and I have to bite my lip to keep from laughing out loud.

Paloma was ten, and in her sparkly blue recital dress, holding her violin, she felt like the most important person in the world. She was the last to go on. Her teacher, Mrs. Lindgren, had told her that's where they put the best player. She stood in the hallway outside the auditorium, bouncing up and down on her toes, humming the opening of her piece under her breath, her bow tapping out the rhythm against her leg. Through the little window in the door she could see her whole family in the third row: her parents, both grandmas, her baby brother on her uncle's lap, and her abuelo, who had driven six hours to be here and was wearing his best hat. Abuelo saw her face in the window and gave her a huge wink. Paloma giggled and ducked out of sight, then popped up again and waved. When Mrs. Lindgren touched her shoulder and said it was time, Paloma took one big breath, lifted her chin, and walked onto the stage like a queen.

Tavish had busked in the Underground for six years, and now, standing at the side of a festival stage with five thousand people waiting in a muddy field, he couldn't stop laughing under his breath. Somebody had filmed him playing at King's Cross. The video had spread. And here he was, his battered acoustic guitar in his hands, a stagehand clipping a microphone to his collar. The grass smelled of rain and spilled cider. The sun was going down pink behind the crowd, and people were sitting on each other's shoulders, and somewhere near the front a group of girls had made a bedsheet banner with his name painted on it in bright yellow letters. He pointed at it and the stagehand laughed with him. He tuned his low E string one more time out of habit, though it was already perfect. His palms were damp and his heart was hammering, but the feeling in his chest was pure fizzing excitement. When the announcer called him, Tavish jogged out into the lights, raised his guitar over his head, and the field roared.

The box on Winifred's doorstep was the size of a microwave and covered in foreign stamps, and she had not ordered anything. She dragged it inside, puzzled, and slit the tape with her kitchen scissors. Inside, packed in crumpled newspaper printed in Portuguese, was a quilt. A patchwork quilt in every color imaginable, and pinned to it a note: Dear Mrs. Hargreave, you taught me English in 1987 when I was a scared little boy from Recife. My mother made this for you before she died. She always wanted you to have it. With love, Paulo. Winifred sat down on the hall floor beside the box. Her hands went to her mouth. Little Paulo, with his huge eyes and his habit of drawing birds in the margins of every worksheet. She pulled the quilt out and buried her face in it, laughing, and found that one of the squares was embroidered with a small blue bird. She wrapped it around her shoulders right there on the floor and sat in it for an hour, smiling, reading the note over and over.

A package showed up at my apartment with no return address, just my name in handwriting I didn't recognize. I shook it. Something rattled. Inside was a jar of homemade mango pickle, wrapped in three layers of bubble wrap and a plastic bag, and a note from my aunt in Hyderabad, whom I hadn't spoken to since my wedding. Your mother told me you've been missing home food. This is your grandmother's recipe. Eat it slowly. I unscrewed the lid and the smell punched me straight in the heart: mustard seed, fenugreek, chili, sour mango. I was suddenly eight years old on my grandmother's veranda in the hot afternoon. I laughed out loud in my empty kitchen. I made a pot of rice immediately, even though it was ten at night, and stood at the counter eating it straight from the pot with a heap of the pickle, burning my mouth, eyes watering, grinning like a madwoman. Then I called my aunt. It was morning there. She picked up and before I could say anything she said, "So? It arrived?"

Leroy Washington, eighty-seven, did not get much mail besides bills and church bulletins, so the package on his porch made him squint suspiciously through his bifocals. He carried it to the kitchen table and opened it with a butter knife. Inside, nestled in tissue paper, was a baseball, yellowed and scuffed, and a photograph of a skinny Black kid in a Negro League uniform, grinning wide. Him. In 1954. There was a letter from a museum curator in Kansas City: the ball had been found in a collector's estate, his signature still faint on the leather, and they thought he ought to have it back, and would he consider coming to speak at their next event? Leroy turned the ball in his gnarled hands. He could still feel how it had come off his bat that day, the crack of it. He let out a low whistle, then a chuckle, then a full laugh that rattled up from his chest. He called his great-grandson and said, "Boy, you remember all those stories you said I made up? Get over here."

I came home from a terrible shift at the hospital to find a box on my doorstep with a children's drawing taped to the top: a stick figure in blue scrubs with enormous yellow hair, holding hands with a smaller stick figure. Underneath it said THANK YOU NURSE SAOIRSE. I knew immediately. Little Matthias, the six-year-old with the burst appendix who'd been so frightened he wouldn't let go of my hand the whole first night. I sat down on my front step without even taking my coat off and opened it. Inside were a dozen chocolate chip cookies, obviously baked by a child, lumpy and slightly burnt on the bottoms, and a card from his parents. Matthias was home, healthy, back in school, and he had insisted on making the cookies himself. I bit into one. It was much too salty, and absolutely perfect. All the exhaustion of the day just lifted off me, and I sat there eating cookie after cookie, laughing at the drawing, holding it up to admire my enormous yellow hair.

Ximena ripped the brown paper off the package standing in the lobby of her building, too curious to wait for the elevator. She hadn't ordered anything. Under the paper was a vinyl record, a first pressing of a Mexican bolero album from 1962, the exact one her father used to play every Sunday morning while he made chilaquiles. The record that had warped in the flood when she was a teenager, that she had looked for in every used shop for fifteen years. A sticky note on the sleeve said, Found it! Sorry it is late for your birthday. Love, your annoying brother. Ximena laughed so loud the doorman looked up from his newspaper. She hugged the record to her chest and practically skipped into the elevator. In her apartment she dug her old turntable out of the closet, blew the dust off the needle, and set the record spinning. The first crackly notes came through the speakers and she spun around her living room with her eyes closed, swaying, singing along in her father's off-key way, holding an imaginary partner.

The mail carrier handed me a soft lumpy package addressed in my daughter's handwriting, and I couldn't think what it could be. She's in her first year at university in Glasgow, broke as anything. I opened it at the garden gate. Out tumbled a scarf, hand-knitted, deep green with uneven stripes, and some dropped stitches she hadn't fixed, and a little note that said, I learned to knit! It took me six weeks. Don't laugh at the holes. I laughed at the holes. I laughed with my whole body, standing on the path in my slippers, and then I wrapped it round my neck twice and it smelled faintly of her shampoo. My neighbor Bernadette was out pruning her roses and asked what had come, and I showed her, turning around to model it like it was haute couture. She clapped. I wore it all afternoon in the garden even though it was sunny and much too warm, and when my husband came home he found me still wearing it at the dinner table, refusing to take it off.

Rhiannon and her brother Gethin had been sorting through Nain's bedroom for an hour when Gethin opened the bottom drawer of the wardrobe and burst out laughing. "Rhi. Rhi, come here." The drawer was crammed full of every school photo they'd ever had taken, every one, including the ones they'd begged their mum to throw away. Rhiannon's year-seven photo, with the fringe she'd cut herself. Gethin's, with the braces and the frosted tips. Their grandmother had framed some of the worst ones. Rhiannon sank down on the carpet, wheezing. Gethin held one up next to his face for comparison, pulling the same goofy expression, and she laughed so hard she had to lie flat on her back. Underneath the photos they found a notebook where Nain had written down every funny thing they'd said as kids, with dates. They took turns reading the entries aloud in her voice, her sing-song Welsh lilt, and each one set them off again. By teatime they had sorted nothing at all, and neither of them minded one bit.

My sisters and I were going through Grandma Lucille's closet when Patrice pulled out a garment bag and unzipped it and gasped. Inside was a sequined jumpsuit, gold, with flared legs and a plunging neckline. None of us had ever seen it. Grandma Lucille was a church organist who wore cardigans and sensible shoes. Then my youngest sister, Bettina, found the photograph pinned inside the bag: Grandma at maybe twenty-five, in that jumpsuit, on a disco floor, mid-spin, her arms flung wide and her head thrown back. We screamed. We actually screamed, all three of us, and then we were rolling around on her bed laughing until our faces were wet. Patrice put the jumpsuit on over her jeans, which was absurd, and struck the pose from the photo. Bettina found Grandma's old record player and an Earth, Wind & Fire album in the hall closet, and we put it on and danced around her bedroom in our socks, the three of us, the needle skipping every time we jumped, the afternoon sun pouring through the lace curtains.

The three brothers had expected the job of clearing out Oma's house to be grim. Instead, Florian kept finding notes. Every drawer, every jar, every cookie tin had a small slip of paper inside, in their grandmother's tidy script. In the sugar canister: Klaus, stop stealing sugar cubes, I can see you. In the sewing kit: Florian, you still owe me a button. In the toolbox: Konrad, this hammer is not a toy, and you know why. The brothers kept calling each other over, holding up each new slip, howling with laughter. Klaus, the eldest, a serious banker in a pressed shirt, laughed so hard at the sugar cube note that he had to sit down on the kitchen floor. She had known everything. Every crime of their childhood. They began hunting for the notes on purpose, tearing through the house like kids on an Easter egg hunt, shouting out each discovery. By evening they had found forty-three. They spread them out on her kitchen table under the lamp and sat around it with mugs of her strong black coffee, still grinning.

My brother Anselm and I were in Nonna's cellar, sorting jars of preserves we'd never be able to eat, when he knocked over a crate and it split open and out spilled dozens of lottery tickets. Hundreds, maybe. All from the 1990s, rubber-banded into bundles by year. We stared at each other. Nonna, who scolded us for wasting money on gum. Anselm picked up a bundle and started reading the numbers out loud, and I realized every single ticket used the same six numbers: our birthdays, our parents' birthdays, and hers. I started to laugh, and then he did, and we couldn't stop. We sat on the cold cellar floor with tickets everywhere like confetti. He found a little notebook in the crate where she'd tracked every draw for thirty years. Near the end she had written, in shaky pencil, Never won. Didn't matter. Every week I got to write their names. That's when we really lost it. We went upstairs carrying the crate between us, still giggling, and bought a ticket that evening, with her numbers.

Yetunde and her twin brother Kayode found the cassette tapes in a shoebox at the back of Mama Agba's wardrobe, each labeled in marker: Yetunde singing, age 4. Kayode's first joke. Twins arguing about rice, 1996. They looked at each other and grinned, and Kayode ran out to the car to dig up the old cassette player their father kept in the trunk. They sat cross-legged on their grandmother's bed and pressed play. The tape hissed, and then out came a tiny squeaky voice, unmistakably Yetunde, warbling a hymn completely off-key, and in the background their grandmother's deep laugh. Yetunde clapped both hands over her face. Kayode fell sideways onto the pillows, kicking his feet. They played them all. The joke was terrible; it was about a goat. The rice argument went on for nine minutes and they were both shrieking in it. Every time their grandmother's voice came through the little speaker, they went quiet and leaned toward it, smiling, and then she would laugh, and they would laugh with her, like she was right there in the room.

Grandma Ruth's recipe box was the last thing left in the kitchen, and my sister Naomi and I fought over it, gently, the way we used to fight over the last latke. Then we decided to go through it together, right there at her yellow Formica table. Every card was annotated. Next to the brisket she'd written: Sol says too much garlic. Sol is wrong. Next to the rugelach: Naomi ate six, got sick, asked for more. Naomi turned bright red and I nearly fell off my chair. The chocolate cake card just said: Make for the girls whenever they are sad. Or not sad. Just make it. So we did. We found her old mixing bowl in the cabinet, the chipped blue one, and her flour was still in the canister, and we made a mess everywhere. Naomi got cocoa on her nose and I didn't tell her for an hour. The kitchen filled with the smell of Grandma's house, which it was, and when the cake came out we ate it warm, with our fingers, laughing, straight from the pan.

Ignatius rolled up the steel shutter of his bookshop at 7:45 on Monday morning, whistling, and stopped mid-note. Taped to the glass door was a sheet of construction paper covered in crayon: WE LOVE YOUR STORE, with a drawing of a dragon reading a book, signed by the second-grade class from the school down the street, the one that had visited on Friday for story hour. He laughed out loud on the empty sidewalk. He peeled it carefully off the door, went inside, flicked on the lights, and taped it right up on the wall behind the register where every customer would see it. Then he went about opening up with an unusual bounce in his step. He watered the fern. He put on a pot of coffee and turned the radio to the jazz station. He straightened the children's section, and while he was there he pulled out a few dragon books and arranged them face-out in a little display, humming. When his first customer came in, a sleepy student, Ignatius greeted her so warmly that she blinked and then smiled back.

I unlocked the café at six on Monday morning and the first thing I did was check the overnight orders, the way I always do, expecting the usual two or three. There were sixty-four. Some food blogger had posted about our cardamom morning buns over the weekend, and the internet had lost its mind. I stood there in my coat in the dark kitchen staring at the screen, and then I started laughing and couldn't stop. Two years I'd been barely scraping by. Two years of my husband asking gently if maybe it was time to sell. I called him and said, "Turn on your phone and look," and heard him yell. Then I put on my apron, put on a playlist full of old Motown, and started rolling dough, singing along at the top of my lungs, flour flying everywhere. My baker, Consuelo, came in at six-thirty, saw the numbers, and screamed, and then we were both singing and rolling, dancing around each other, and the kitchen filled with the smell of butter and cardamom and coffee as the sun came up.

Mr. Phan had run the corner hardware store for thirty years, and every Monday he opened it the same way: unlock the door, flip the sign, sweep the step, put the kettle on. This Monday, as he bent to sweep the step, he found an envelope with his name on it tucked under the mat. Inside was a twenty-dollar bill and a note. Fifteen years ago I stole a pocketknife from your store. I was twelve and stupid. I'm a carpenter now, and I buy my tools from you every week, and I've been too embarrassed to say. I'm sorry. Thank you for always being kind to me. Mr. Phan read it twice, leaning on his broom, and started to chuckle, shaking his head. He knew exactly who it was; the tall young man who always asked about his grandchildren. He folded the note into his shirt pocket, finished sweeping, and put the kettle on, still chuckling. When the young man came in at ten for nails, Mr. Phan handed him a pocketknife from the display case, wrapped in tissue, and winked.

Monday mornings had always been the worst part of the week at the flower shop. But this Monday, Constance pulled up and found a line. An actual line of people on the sidewalk outside her door at 7:50, ten minutes before opening. She stared at them through her windshield, then looked down at her phone and remembered: the local paper had run the story about her shop yesterday. The headline had called her the flower lady who saved Elm Street. She hadn't thought anyone would read it. She got out of the car with her face going hot and pink, and an older man at the front of the line started clapping, and then everybody did. Constance laughed and flapped her hands at them to stop, fumbling with the keys, dropping them, picking them up, laughing harder. When she finally got the door open, the bell jingled and people streamed in, admiring the peonies and the ranunculus. She spent the whole morning wrapping bouquets, chatting, ringing up sales, so busy her cheeks hurt from smiling, and she didn't stop to eat until two o'clock.

There's a bell over my shop door that my father hung in 1979, and every Monday when I open up, I give it a flick for luck. Today I flicked it and it rang and I just stood there in the doorway grinning, because today my daughter starts working here with me. She's twenty-two, she graduated in business last month, and she turned down a job in the city to come home and help run the deli. I didn't ask her to. I would never have asked her to. She walked in at eight in a crisp new apron with her name embroidered on it, which she'd ordered herself, and I had to turn around and fuss with the coffee machine so she wouldn't see my face. We set up the display case together. She arranged the olives better than I ever have. When Mrs. Kaplan came in for her usual pound of pastrami, she saw the two of us behind the counter and clutched her chest and said, "Now that's what I like to see," and my daughter and I looked at each other and laughed.

Aurelio flicked on the lights in his little bicycle repair shop at eight o'clock on Monday morning and found the place transformed. Over the weekend, while he'd been at his cousin's wedding, his nephew and three of his nephew's friends had snuck in with the spare key and painted the whole interior. The grimy gray walls were now a deep sunny yellow. Someone had painted a mural of a bicycle flying over the city skyline on the back wall, and his workbench had been scrubbed clean, every tool hung neatly on a new pegboard. On the counter was a note: SURPRISE, TÍO! Aurelio stood there in the doorway with his keys still dangling from his hand. Then he started laughing, a deep, rumbling laugh that went on and on. He walked around the shop touching everything, the bright walls, the clean bench, the pegboard, shaking his head and saying, "Those rascals, those rascals." He called his nephew, who was clearly waiting by the phone, and they both laughed so much neither could get a proper sentence out.

Henrik had been volunteering at the food bank every Saturday for three years, and today they had the biggest delivery he'd ever seen: a whole truckload of fresh produce donated by a farm upstate. He was up to his elbows in crates of apples, peaches, sweet corn, and enormous heads of lettuce, sorting them onto tables, and he couldn't stop smiling. The whole warehouse smelled like a summer orchard. When the doors opened, the families came in and their faces changed when they saw the tables. A little boy grabbed a peach and bit straight into it, juice running down his chin, and his mother started to scold him and then started laughing instead. An old woman picked up an ear of corn and held it to her nose and told Henrik she hadn't had fresh corn in two summers. He loaded her bag full. By noon his back ached and his hands were sticky with peach juice and his T-shirt was soaked through, and he felt lighter than he had all year. He hummed through cleanup, then went home and called the farm to say thank you.

I'd been assigned to the bread table at the food bank, which sounded boring until I realized it meant I got to talk to every single person who came through the line. A little girl in a pink raincoat asked me very seriously which bread was the softest. I squeezed every loaf on the table like a scientist and handed her the winner, and she squeezed it too and nodded with great approval. A construction worker told me a terrible joke about a baguette and I laughed so hard I snorted, which made him laugh even harder. An older Vietnamese couple brought me a container of homemade spring rolls as a thank you, which I wasn't supposed to accept, so I ate one very quickly behind the table when the coordinator wasn't looking. By the end of the shift I knew a dozen people's names, my face ached from smiling, and I'd made plans to come back next week. Walking to my car afterward, I realized I'd forgotten to check my phone for four hours straight. I couldn't remember the last time that had happened.

Sixteen-year-old Delfina had only signed up to volunteer at the food bank because her school required community service hours. But by her third Saturday, she was the first one there, waiting outside with her coffee before the director, Mr. Okonkwo, even arrived with the keys. She loved the rhythm of it: unloading boxes, stacking cans by type, chatting with the regulars as they came through. She had learned that Mr. Halvorsen liked to have his canned peaches in a separate bag so they wouldn't bruise his bread. She knew the Nguyen kids' names and their favorite cereals. Today, a woman she'd helped the very first week came in and hugged her. She had gotten a job, she said, a good one, and she wouldn't need to come anymore, but she had wanted to say thank you in person. Delfina hugged her back, hard, and her eyes stung, and she was grinning so wide it hurt. She spent the rest of the shift humming, and when Mr. Okonkwo asked her what was up, she just shrugged and kept on smiling.

We'd been worried for weeks that the food bank would run short before Thanksgiving, and on Friday morning I came in to find the loading dock stacked to the ceiling. Turkeys. Dozens of them, frozen solid, plus sacks of potatoes and cases of cranberry sauce. A local high school football team had organized a drive and delivered it all overnight. I just stood there in the cold with my hands on top of my head, laughing in disbelief. The other volunteers came in one by one and each one stopped in the doorway and did the same thing. Our coordinator, Brunhilde, a gruff woman who never smiled, burst into tears and then started laughing at herself for crying. We got to work, hauling, sorting, writing out names, cracking jokes the whole time. Somebody put on music. Somebody started a turkey-carrying relay race. By the time the families started arriving, we were giddy, all of us, wishing every single person a wonderful holiday, and I meant it more than I have ever meant anything I said to a stranger.

Lars was eighty-four and moved slowly, so the food bank had given him the easiest job: sitting at the welcome table with a clipboard, signing people in. He had expected to be bored. Instead he discovered that he was very good at it. He remembered everyone. He asked after their grandchildren, their bad knees, their job interviews, the score of their kids' soccer games. He kept a bowl of butterscotch candies on the table and handed them out to anyone who looked like they needed one, which, in his opinion, was everyone. Today a young father came in with a baby in a carrier, looking exhausted, and Lars told him a story about his own first baby, sixty years ago, who had cried for eleven months straight and grew up to be a judge. The young man laughed, really laughed, for the first time Lars had seen. Lars felt a warm glow spread through his chest and all the way out to his stiff fingers. He handed the man two butterscotch candies instead of one and winked.

Saturday at the food bank, and I was on the kids' table, where we hand out little bags of snacks and a free book to every child who comes in. A boy of maybe seven came up and looked at the books for a long time, very serious, and finally asked if we had anything about sharks. We did. One. A big glossy picture book about great whites. When I handed it to him, his whole face exploded into a smile, and he hugged the book to his chest and spun around to show his mom, yelling, "Mama, SHARKS!" She laughed and mouthed thank you at me. Ten minutes later I looked over and he was sitting on the floor by the door, reading it aloud to his little sister, doing shark noises, which, I learned, sound a lot like a growly whisper. I couldn't stop watching him. The other volunteers kept catching me grinning at nothing. On my way home I stopped at a bookstore and bought every shark book they had, and dropped them off at the food bank the next morning.

Silas had been sitting in the maternity waiting room for six hours, through two vending machine coffees and an entire bag of pretzels, when the nurse finally came through the double doors and said his name. He leaped up so fast he knocked his chair over. "Mother and baby are both doing great," she said, smiling. "You've got a granddaughter." Silas grabbed the nurse's hand and shook it hard with both of his. Then, realizing he was still shaking it, he let go and laughed at himself, a big booming laugh that made the other people in the waiting room look up and smile. He turned to the man sitting across from him, a total stranger who'd been waiting almost as long, and told him the news, and the stranger clapped him on the back. When Silas was finally allowed into the room and saw his daughter in the bed, worn out but radiant, holding a tiny pink bundle, he had to stop in the doorway and catch his breath. His daughter held the baby out. He took her, and his face just crumpled into a grin.

I'd been in the surgical waiting room since seven in the morning, watching the status board, where my husband was listed only as a number. Patient 4471: In Surgery. For hours it didn't change. I'd read the same paragraph of my book thirty times. Then, at 1:15, the board flickered, and the line changed to: Patient 4471: In Recovery. I actually gasped. A minute later the surgeon came out, still in her cap, and sat beside me and said the words I'd been praying for: the tumor was out, all of it, clean margins, and he was going to be fine. I grabbed her hands and said thank you about ten times. My voice wouldn't stay steady. Once she left, I laughed out loud, sitting there all alone, and the woman knitting across from me looked up and smiled like she understood. I called our kids, one after another, and with each call I laughed again, because I kept hearing the news new each time I said it. When they let me in to see him, he was groggy and grumpy and asking for ice chips, and I'd never seen anything so wonderful.

Ngozi sat in the emergency waiting room with her eight-year-old son, Chidi, who had fallen off the monkey bars and was holding his arm very still against his chest. She had been preparing herself for the worst for an hour. When the doctor finally came out with the X-ray, she said it was just a minor sprain, nothing broken, and then she held up the scan to the light and showed Chidi the bones in his own wrist. He leaned in, fascinated, his pain forgotten. "Those are mine? Inside me?" The doctor laughed and said yes, and asked if he wanted to keep a copy. Chidi's eyes went enormous. Ngozi felt her shoulders drop about three inches and a laugh bubble up from deep in her belly. Her son was fine. Her son was going to show the entire class his skeleton. In the car on the way home, Chidi held the printout up to the window, studying his own bones with total wonder, and told her he was going to be a doctor now. Ngozi grinned at him in the rearview mirror the whole drive.

The waiting room at the transplant center has an ugly orange carpet and a fish tank with exactly one very old goldfish. I'd spent so much time staring at that fish over the past two years that I'd named him Gerald. Today I was there with my brother, Ambrose, who was getting his final checkup six months after he gave me one of his kidneys. We were both there to hear whether everything was still working. The doctor came out and said the most beautiful sentence I've ever heard: "You two are the most boring patients I have. Everything's perfect." Ambrose and I looked at each other and both burst out laughing, and he put me in a headlock right there in the waiting room like we were kids, and a nurse yelled at him to be careful with my incision, which made us laugh harder. On the way out, I stopped at the fish tank and tapped the glass and said goodbye to Gerald, and promised him I would not be seeing him again for a very, very long time.

Ludmila had come to the hospital waiting room expecting a long night: her husband, Pavel, had collapsed at dinner and the paramedics had muttered something about his heart. She sat clutching his coat in her lap, staring at the doors. Then Pavel himself came walking out through them, still in a hospital gown with his trousers pulled on underneath, holding a paper that said he'd fainted because of low blood sugar and dehydration and nothing more. He'd skipped lunch and run around in the garden all afternoon in the heat. "I am an old fool," he announced to the entire waiting room, throwing his arms wide. Ludmila jumped up and swatted his arm with his coat, and then threw it over his shoulders and hugged him, laughing so hard she couldn't speak. The other people in the waiting room were chuckling too. A security guard applauded. On the way to the parking lot, she bought him two candy bars from the vending machine and made him eat both of them right there in the hallway while she watched, giggling the whole time.

I'm sitting in the waiting room of the rehab wing, and in about five minutes my best friend, Thaddeus, is going to walk out of those double doors on his own two feet for the first time since the accident last winter. His physical therapist called me yesterday and told me to come, said he wanted me there. I've brought balloons. Too many balloons, honestly; the nurse at the desk raised her eyebrows at me. My leg is bouncing so hard the chair is squeaking, and I keep standing up and sitting back down. A little old man across the room asks who I'm waiting for, and I end up telling him the whole story, eight months of it, the surgeries, the setbacks, the stupid jokes we made at three in the morning to keep from crying. He nods along and grins with me. Then the doors swing open, and there's Thaddeus, gripping a cane, wobbling, but upright and walking, and he sees the balloons and rolls his eyes and laughs, and I'm already halfway across the room.
